A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SEAL and share identifiable methods, experiments and results. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive rewriting and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original pruning experiments, retrieval evaluations, context-extension experiments, LongBench and MMLU results, and sample-count/learning-rate analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and additionally reports RULER evaluations, cross-task transfer measurements and one-shot prompting comparisons.

M1.justification: Both versions generate task-formatted training examples and learn head-wise or channel-wise attention-output scales. Offline merging already appears in v1. v2's expanded merging explanation, including grouped-query attention, documents implementation rather than establishing a changed procedure. SEAL-L/SEAL-D correspond to the retained LoRA/DoRA comparators.

E1.justification: v2 adds RULER variable tracking, common word extraction and frequent word extraction, substantially extending task requirements beyond the previous evaluations. Line retrieval, Needle-in-a-Haystack, MMLU and LongBench document QA remain represented. Naming triviaqa_e for LongBench training supplies previously missing documentation rather than establishing a dataset replacement.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds one-shot prompting for LongChat-7B and Vicuna-13B. LoRA/DoRA line-retrieval comparisons are reduced from five models to those two; the Mistral-7B, Vicuna-7B and LongChat-13B comparison rows disappear. The five-model Needle-in-a-Haystack LoRA/DoRA comparison remains in Appendix G, so that relocation is not a comparator removal.

E3.justification: New RULER protocols introduce Llama-3.1-8B, 200 evaluation samples per task, testing up to 64K and variable-length training samples. The one-shot comparison uses a 1K-token example and maximum task lengths of 30K/15K, versus 31K/16K in the primary table. Mistral SEAL-C's reported Needle-in-a-Haystack learning rate changes from 4e-4 in v1 Appendix A to 4e-2 in v2 Table 4; rerunning is not established.

E4.justification: v2 replaces line-retrieval-to-LongBench transfer evaluation with a RULER task-to-task transfer analysis. It also removes the MLP-specific direct-effect analysis from the retained retrieval error case. The pruning experiments, MMLU check and sample-count/learning-rate ablations remain; moving the latter to Appendix E does not add an analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new RULER evaluation sample count describes evaluation size, not repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds RULER, one-shot and cross-task transfer results, including Llama-3.1-8B's 64K CWE scores of 0.1 for baseline and 95.7 for SEAL-C. LongBench SEAL-H averages change from 33.52/26.23 to 33.25/26.05, while its out-of-domain rows disappear. Parameter counts also change, including 13B SEAL-C from 207.7K to 204.8K. Primary baseline/SEAL line-retrieval scores remain unchanged; the shorter-context comparison is not a same-setting improvement.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 2 introduces a formal transferability metric: summed score changes across lengths normalized by the baseline score range. The existing direct-effect equation is retained with clearer unembedding-weight notation. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The central claims of inexpensive attention scaling, improved retrieval and compatibility with context extension remain. v2 removes the abstract's explicit claim of considerable out-of-domain improvement and the conclusion's generalization claim, while prioritizing synthetic rule-based retrieval and retaining LongBench as additional validation.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the broad generalization interpretation with task-dependent transfer: scales learned on word-extraction tasks can harm variable tracking, motivating category-specific training. Its mechanism explanation omits v1's dominant-MLP account and the caveat that pruning effects might reflect format understanding. New limitations discuss memory requirements for longer training sequences and task-dependent learning-rate tuning.

D1.justification: v2 specifies selection of the 50 longest triviaqa_e samples for LongBench, documents RULER data generation and learning rates, and explains offline-merging axes and grouped-query attention. Most existing optimizer, hardware, sample-generation and training-budget information is retained. Conversely, v1's explicit LongBench-specific learning rates are omitted.

R1.justification: The research context is substantially narrowed toward synthetic retrieval benchmarks, with circuit-analysis and context-extension discussion partly redistributed. v2 adds RULER, GQA and Llama 3 references while removing Wu et al.'s retrieval-head work and much of the hallucination, RAG and chain-of-thought background. LongBench's publication update represents the same cited work.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, motivation and method explanations. It nests qualitative analysis within experiments, creates separate comparison sections, relocates LongBench discussion to Appendix D and reorganizes the appendices. These changes substantially alter the narrative and structure of retained material.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figures 2–4 are reorganized or redrawn, including an offline-merging diagram and replacement of flattened head plots with three-dimensional plots. The context-extension table becomes Figure 6, the full Needle-in-a-Haystack comparison moves to Appendix G, and new RULER and transfer displays are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and qualifies applicability through harder RULER tasks, a newer long-context model, a relevant prompting comparator and explicit negative-transfer evidence. These address gaps in v1's support for broad retrieval and generalization claims. LongBench data-selection details and practical limitations also improve transparency. These gains outweigh the loss of MLP-specific analysis, several line-retrieval comparator results and some reproducibility details.
